Clausi’s passion

If Clausi’s recall to Rome had the immediate purpose of presenting him to Pope Pius IX, who wished to meet him, it was not a formal obedience, as we have said, and he waited for precise instructions. Meanwhile he looked after the College of the Monti in place of the councillors[1] or Assistants who had gone with the Superior General to the March of Ancona. He thought and hoped, as he said explicitly, that he could return to Paterno, where the community of the Sanctuary he had restored kept asking to have him back, not least because work still remained to be done. But the deeper reason was another: he had resolved on solitude and retirement, given the spiritual affliction he had been in for some months.

The capital of Catholicism, with its well-known many demands of sacred ministry and religious service in church and outside, did not help him to settle. A painful passion, which he himself would call a “storm”,[2] had indeed begun for him and became obvious to all. He had scarcely arrived at Saint Francis of Paola ai Monti when the brethren there noticed the first signs.

“I noticed at once the change that had come over him,” Fr. Mantuano would testify.[3]

Because of the strain of the journey and the bad weather, the brethren made sure he took some necessary refreshment, but Fr. Bernardo, though grateful, reproached himself for allowing it. Moreover, from the same first-hand source we learn that in the days that followed he would go weeping through the dormitories of the convent, breaking out in cries of regret:

Everyone understood the meaning of the trial to which his inconsolable soul was subjected. His experience was like purgatory, almost hell, with this difference from hell: the torment of feeling abandoned by God was joined to an anxious search for him as the one true and supreme Good.

Among the first to come and encourage him, but in vain, was Don Vincenzo Pallotti, his friend, the holy priest and founder, who invited him to spend a week together in the Camaldolese peace near Tusculum for his spirit’s relief.[5] The Pope too, in whom Clausi had confided, played his part as consoling angel, as he admits:

“I spent a week with Pallotti at the Camaldoli above Frascati. The Pope truly confided in me like an Angel of the Lord. But none of these things give me any pleasure if I do not find God, for the usual desolations continue, and I gave the Pope a detailed account of them, telling him that for many years I have found no fervour, except on the feast of Saint Francis de Sales last year.”[6]

Although he often examined his conscience and went to confession and found no matter of certain guilt in himself, no words could comfort him, whoever spoke them.

In the same letter he writes: “Although examining my conscience I do not think I have committed any grave sin knowingly, and I could attribute the cause to my failure to respond and my infidelity to the abundance of past graces, gifts and favours. He told me it was general and that God is silent with all souls.”[7]

“It was remarkable, however,” Fr. Mantuano would testify, “that while he was in this great anguish and desolation of spirit, he was nevertheless very precise in advising others and dispelling their doubts.”[8]

Heaven’s silence towards him was painful indeed, made of both darkness and dryness, for one who had long known their opposite. So Fr. Bernardo never tired of asking and begging for prayers for even a faint return of light and fervour.

“I beg you not to stop praying or having others pray for me,” he urged the confrere closest to him in spirit, Fr. Martini, “so that the Lord may give me a little

Alongside his spiritual sufferings, Clausi’s bodily health was sorely tried. An intermittent stomach complaint afflicted him with sometimes piercing pain, but for him it was not the greatest evil. On 2 March he described it thus:

“Last night I was very ill, with such fierce pain that I thought I would die… Unless [God] himself deigns to work a miracle, it seems impossible to be cured by human means…”[11] And he adds: “I abandon myself at the holy feet of Mary, Mother of Graces and Mercies, whom I always keep at the head of my bed. If the Lord wants to take my life, I make him not one but a thousand sacrifices of myself, but may his most holy and divine Will be done.”[12]

In August, as the trouble worsened, he reported:

“I feel very ill and as usual I often have to vomit at night, without sleeping, so my strength keeps failing.”[13]

12 Ibid., Letter to Fr. L. Martini, same date. 13 Ibid., Letter to Fr. R. Sbano, 16 Aug. 1848.

But there was an evil that afflicted him more than the physical one: “wicked tongues”. No one is spared them, and neither was he. He complained of them to his friend and confidant:

“Between ourselves,” he wrote to Fr. Martini, “I can no longer keep from telling you that among my spiritual anguish, which comes from God and which everyone here tells me is a special grace, though I do not deserve it… diabolical tongues have not been lacking…, and these pierce my heart more than ever, because by God’s mercy I have never had a thought of consenting to any temptation; indeed I think I have used (sic) every possible means for God to free me from sin, as I hope he has.”[14]

These were only malicious rumours that reached Fr. Bernardo’s ears, but that was enough for him to reaffirm his sincerity and integrity.[15]

If it is true, as it is, that fervour of spirit cannot be quenched by a flood of physical and moral trials, the trial of passive purification that Fr. Bernardo experienced was, as all persons of sure virtue affirmed, among the most painful. So held Saint Vincent Pallotti, who knew him better than anyone and saw him often.

“Ah no, that is a martyrdom!” he replied to anyone who voiced the slightest suspicion about Clausi’s mental state,[16] adding by way of explanation: “Fr. Bernardo is now in a state of very great light, in which he sees God full of holiness and perfection and himself as a monster.”[17] And to Clausi himself he said, for comfort and guidance: “All the pains you suffer are for your greater glory in the next life.”[18]

Others experienced in virtue and perfection said the same.

“To gauge to some extent what his sufferings were at such times, one must remember that this was the man who before this trial had shown such love for the most august Sacrament… and suddenly he believed himself deprived of this love, indeed of God himself”:[19] “it is one of the greatest trials God sends his Servants, testing them like gold in the crucible, in the fire of the greatest and most painful tribulations, to unite them more closely to himself.”[20]

It is also found in the teaching of the spiritual masters, beginning, as we have seen, with the Mystical Doctor Saint John of the Cross.

“It is a painful disturbance,” he says, “of many suspicions, imaginings and conflicts within the soul, in which it sees itself, suspects and fears that it is lost and that its blessings are gone for ever. Hence such deep pain and groaning enter its spirit that it utters loud spiritual roars and cries.”[21]

Scaramelli for his part calls them “extreme afflictions” and “inner pains of death”,[22] pains which Cardinal Bona describes as “like the pains of hell”.[23]

But let us read Fr. Bernardo himself, in his first-hand experience.

Unable to find in himself any direct responsibility for this experience, he asked himself:

“But what can it have been, that without realising it I have fallen out of God’s grace?”[24] And he also remarked: “They think I have lost my mind… but it is the trial through which God wants to lead me.”[25]

Yet he never complained of Providence’s dealings with him, but with ever greater awareness and strength exclaimed:

If he grieved, and grieved greatly, it was for fear of being the cause, though he could not identify it in specific faults or details. With no objective confirmation, yet with the afflicting, dark and incomprehensible reality persisting, he was driven to the subjective conviction that he was somehow responsible, even blaming himself for what he had always knowingly excluded from his life.

He himself gives us an idea of what was happening in his soul in a letter written on 1 April 1848, after celebrating Mass at the Chiesa Nuova in the chapel of his favourite saint, Philip Neri.

“I feel a certainty in my heart and see all its effects, and I draw the certain, indeed most certain, conclusion that by my cursed sins, my diabolical malice, the envy of Cain, vengeance, arrogance and rashness… I have drawn (sic) upon myself all the curses of Psalm 108.”[27]

To those who pitied him in his affliction he would repeat: “Quis agnovit vias Domini? aut quis consiliarius Eius fuit?”[28]

Yet, and this is an incontestable sign of continuing theological life and union with God, he did not swerve in the least from prayer and penance, which he even multiplied, nor from his visibly blameless conduct, all the more heroic for being so tried, and most edifying in its humility and conformity to God’s will. More than that: he was seen to grow in aspirations, ejaculatory prayers, sighs and outpourings of love for God, sometimes prostrate on the step of the Blessed Sacrament altar, remaining there long in fervent adoration.[29] One can truly say that the many waters of tribulation could not quench the love of God dwelling in his spirit; or, like a volcano covered in snow in harsh winter, the incandescent magma still seethed within.

Moreover, he was assiduous in his monastic duties and observances as long as some remnant of strength allowed; he was most punctual in choir for the divine praises; he celebrated Mass with intense fervour and went to confession often and in tears. When he could not celebrate, since this comfort too failed him because he thought himself utterly unworthy, he attended two or three Masses, and grew in his desire to approach Jesus in the Sacrament and in the practice of the virtues.[30]

But most wonderful of all, while he found no peace for himself and kept pleading:

“Give me my God and I am cured,” or “Who will give me my God? O my God, let me see your face!”,[31] he perfectly reassured the other souls who still came to him for comfort and advice in their trials or help in their needs.[32] For in his sufferings, partly from God, such as the withdrawal of consolation and of the feeling or experience of his life of grace, and partly from the devil, by God’s permission as with holy Job, such as fear and terror, the suggestion that he had irremediably lost God through his own fault, together with spiritual and bodily torment, Fr. Bernardo was like one who lives in himself but not for himself, as Tornatore would explain: in God’s eyes he lived by grace and in strength, but was not aware of it, so that alongside the ecstasy of love for God there was the ecstasy of anguish at being rejected by him.[33]

Such spiritual affliction did not spare Clausi’s body from accompanying physical suffering and emaciation. His stomach troubles returned more violently; his face and whole body showed clear signs of wasting.[34] So his confreres thought it best to move him temporarily, sending him in the summer to S. Andrea delle Fratte for some change.[35] From S. Andrea he went to S. Salvatore in Onda, to the holy Pallotti, and gained some improvement, saying he was “somewhat relieved, per viscera misericordiae Dei nostri”.[36] But it was very little, since that same day, 5 September 1848, he wrote to Caracciolo of Falconara Albanese:

We do not know whether this journey took place,

“My stomach is bad as usual, and I am afflicted in spirit by the great fear of having lost God… But I want to hope.”[37]

Clausi’s hope returns as a constant theme even in the darkest and most anguished hours.

“If the Lord has to work a miracle,” he remarked, “he will do it to save me, because he shed his blood for me”; and he sealed the statement by repeating: “Copiosa apud eum redemptio.”[38]

A further cause of inner tribulation came to Clausi from the outward afflictions and tribulations of the Church; he shared in them intensely as in her passion, with his own passion; indeed he lived his own in relation to hers, calling himself the one truly responsible, the antichrist, while renewing his self-offering as a victim for the end of her tribulation.[39]

Fr. Tornatore, who visited him with admirable and sincere veneration, edified by his outstanding virtues and charismatic gifts, modestly reports in the third person confidences he presumably received from Clausi himself:

“He told a confidant that from childhood his heart had been the echo of the Church’s ills. The Church’s ills are her pain and groans at her children going astray. He added that the Church’s ills, already great in his days of ’48, would reach their height, as had been revealed to him.”[40]

To Fr. Bernardo, as we have said,

“the Church’s ills and the infinite mercies that were to follow them had been revealed many times, and he prayed the Lord to hasten those blessed times of the Church by soon ending the ills that afflicted her”.[41]

That was why he had offered himself to God as a victim of expiation for the people’s sins, that God might pardon the wickedness of the world that caused those ills. He had made this offering so spontaneously, generously and simply that he himself compared it to the ease with which, in his day, people took “a little pinch of snuff”.[42]

The Church’s passion

It was not only the personal sins of individuals that brought affliction to the Church, but also collective sins of the people, or rather of fringes or factions of the people.

We have already noted that not all the “hosannas” shouted from the square to Pope Pius IX were sincere and disinterested. Some, linking the name of Pius with that of Charles Albert, stirred up the myth of the “liberal Pope” to prepare political unrest and uprisings in the name of a national patriotism which, though open to discussion, did not hide the real aims of anti-papal and anticlerical theorists and groups. Farini himself, an active and convinced supporter of the constitutional experiment in the Papal States, reproached and accused radicals and Mazzinians of giving the revolution an anti-religious tone.[43] Mixed into the movement for Italian unity was indeed the intention of destroying the Pope’s religious and spiritual power after his political power.

The “government of the people” Mazzini hoped for was to be achieved through the very exiles returning to the Papal States, to stir up trouble and exasperate, to exploit reaction and provoke the worst.

Angelo Brunetti, known as “Ciceruacchio”, organised processions, harangued the crowds and stirred up public discontent. Part of the nobility and part of the people split into clubs, some legalist, others sympathising with and supporting the independence movements. By 1848 feelings were inflamed and a political crisis broke out inside and outside the borders of the State of the Church. To calm people, on 10 February Pius IX issued a proclamation that ended:

“Bless Italy, great God, and preserve for her always this most precious gift of all, the Faith!”

Unfortunately this essentially religious invocation was interpreted and exploited in a clearly political and anti-Austrian sense. It was a misunderstanding, historians comment,[44] but in any event those who wanted unrest got it, and on 15 November 1848 Pellegrino Rossi was assassinated. The Pope, who had thought of leaving Rome the day after the riot, nine days later,

A new proclamation prepared the day before but never published gave the reasons for his departure;[45] another, substantially identical, was published from his voluntary exile on the 27th.

In Rome meanwhile the situation came to a head. First a Junta, then a provisional government and elections to the Constituent Assembly led, on the night of 8-9 February 1848 [sic: 1849], to the proclamation of the Roman Republic, governed from March by the well-known triumvirate of Giuseppe Mazzini, Carlo Armellini (formerly a consistorial advocate) and Aurelio [sic: “Pietro” in the original] Saffi, a republican from Romagna.

It was not a persecution planned by the responsible authorities but abuses committed by fanatics and undisciplined men.

“In Rome,” according to Farini as quoted by Martina, “public order was not seriously disturbed… but there was much clamour, boasting and Jacobin threats… The rebels grew more hostile to priests and friars every day and pursued them in the streets with slanders, so that many… dressed as laymen…”[46]

Between the end of April and early May 1848 [sic: 1849], some ten priests were slaughtered in the convent of San Callisto by the Finance Guards; other acts of violence were committed by the mobilised Civic Guard at Santa Croce; in the streets priests were harassed and insulted by the rabble.[47] Saint Vincent Pallotti too, for his intransigence and zeal, was long sought by the republican police and ran serious risks, as one who had been too often at the Apostolic Palace of the Quirinal.[48]

The Pope, sheltering in the Kingdom of Naples as guest of the Bourbon king, who was proud to put his Royal Palace at Portici at his disposal, long hoped for the Romans’ “desired repentance”[49] and trusted that legality would be restored, certain that the trial that had afflicted the Church, and any others the Lord might send him, would be followed by a great triumph for the Church.[50] Many souls of God agreed in this hope and prophecy of the “triumph of the Church”, among them our Clausi,[51] as we have seen.

“Let us pray,” he said, “that these enemies of Holy Church may be converted and bear fruits worthy of penance.”[53]

From Fr. Tornatore we also learn that during the political revolution of that time in Rome he

“lived in seclusion in his convent, since he was already suffering his anguish of spirit…, but I know personally that to anyone who came to him he gave maxims and teaching on the duty of remaining firm in obedience and respect for the Roman Pontiff”.[54]

“heart was an echo of the various storms to which the Church was subject”, especially the one then raging. He assured them he had made his offering to the Lord, adding:

Inner and outer tribulations piled up in Clausi’s heart, and true to his self-offering as a victim, he “kissed the hand of God that struck him and, acknowledging himself deserving of any punishment, said:

‘God is good and merciful: I am the cause of his anger’; and he often repeated: ‘My God, I want to love you: when shall I find you again, my God! Nothing afflicts me but the misfortune of having lost you!’”[57]

But this is the experience of contemplatives “in valle lacrimarum”, as another man of God, a confrere of Fr. Bernardo and an expert on “troubled souls”, the Servant of God Fr. Nicolas Barré, would say. In it, he says, they are

“drawn to enjoy God, yet believe they do not have him and humble themselves in their unworthiness. They have a treasure without knowing it, despite the most intimate communications and familiarity with God”.[58]

In fact the whole period of Clausi’s great tribulation was one of continual and almost exclusive loving attention and familiarity with God, though “dark” because of the accompanying passive purification of the inner and outer senses. Outwardly, or in his subjective impression, he felt detached and far away, and he feared for his confreres. In August of that year, fearing that he was drawing down divine punishment and causing the tribulations of the Church and of the good people he lived with, he said sadly:

“Some day a thunderbolt will fall on this College and reduce us to ashes; if only it killed me alone, that would not be so bad; then God’s anger would be appeased. I am sorry for all of you, who are innocent and may suffer because of me.” But he immediately added: “The Lord will restore peace to the Church, and blessed are you who will see it.”[59]

In any case it was a new affliction that consumed Fr. Bernardo, yet it contained a consuming passion for the Lord, the Love of his soul. It was afflictive love, proper to the “night” of the spirit, a true passion of divine love. Fear and terror of having offended him caused him extreme anxiety and anguish. So in March 1849 he had someone write to Cardinal Costantino Patrizi, His Holiness’s Vicar, in exile with him at Portici, to obtain absolution for him from any censures he might have incurred. Not only was he reassured on this, but the Pope, through the Cardinal, also granted him the faculty to celebrate privately on Holy Thursday.[60]

The final confrontation

The earthly end of Fr. Bernardo’s life, with the dramatic tones that marked it to the very eve and the glorious close of the human, religious and heroic experience that concluded it, amounts to a decisive confrontation and a verification of him as witness and sign. Not only did Clausi’s charism and mission prove authentic; not only were his predictions confirmed by the final events; but his asceticism and apostolate, his virtue and reputation for holiness perfectly matched those of outstanding Servants of God, in a line and style all his own, made of nature and grace, of divine gifts and initiative and his faithful response. Anyone measuring their inner and outer dimensions by a purely human yardstick would see the appearance of failure, averted at the last moment by the irruption of the Spirit who floods and exalts. But anyone who looks at the theological and moral side of this decisive confrontation finds the victory of one who knew how to believe, hope and love, even in the acute suffering of one of the most original experiences of love and pain, made purer by the convincing witness of a fidelity tested to the utmost. The first victory, however, is God’s, who becomes the reward and crown of his own gifts.

Led along the hard path of the strong, Bernardo Clausi let himself be guided by the hand that drove him along his particular path of holiness, entrusting himself steadfastly to the One “who strikes down and raises up, who afflicts and consoles”. In this lies what is imitable in the witness and sign.

The persistence of his terrible spiritual affliction did not diminish the Father’s fervour of will and virtue; if anything it sharpened it. Prayer, as we know,

“was a continual exercise for him even in the time of his anguish”;[1] and “if there was a time,” Fr. Mantuano would testify, “when I paid more attention to his virtues and considered them truly heroic, it was in the last two years of his life. In the past his liveliness, cheerfulness and ease covered the depth of his virtues and almost made them seem ordinary to me, although they inspired a reverential respect for him; but when I saw him so anguished and reduced, especially in roughly the last two months of his life, to the point of being unable to recite the office, acting only out of obedience, or rather exactly as if forced, then I began to have the highest esteem for his virtue, because it was tested in the fire of tribulation, all the bitterer because its cause was a groundless fear of having lost God.”[2]

The worsening of his stomach complaint meant he could keep down no food or drink. So he grew ever weaker physically, but it was his spiritual desolation that had a terrible effect on his bodily health, and he named the Evil One, whom he called the serpent and infernal dragon,[3] as the immediate cause of the sufferings of both, feeling besieged and harassed by him. “I feel hell in my bowels and the infernal serpent gnawing them.” He explained to those who could not understand his desolation that it was harassment by the Evil One, but immediately added:

“God’s will, God’s permission!”, confirming his words with Scripture: “Who has known the ways (that is, the thought, the mind) of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?”[4]

He knew, at any rate, that God was testing him to perfect him:

“This is the trial through which he wants to lead me.”[5] And he added: “Ah, my God, have pity on me!” “Grant, O Lord, that I may love you.”[6]

Although he felt unworthy to be with the other religious, he took part in community acts as best he could; later, as his physical weakness increased, he no longer could. The others went to visit him, and when they asked how he was he answered sadly but resignedly:

Celebrating Mass was out of the question: not only did he lack the physical strength (it was surprising that he could stand at times despite extreme undernourishment), but also the moral strength, declaring himself utterly unworthy and morally prevented, since, considering himself an infernal monster, he would not knowingly outrage God’s august Majesty. The same with holy communion.

“By God’s grace,” he would answer those who expressed surprise and regret, “I have never celebrated with a single venial sin.”

“What are you doing? My illness is not natural. Give me my God and I shall be well and a Samson.”[14] “Let our Mother act; she will know how to plead for me with her divine Son.”[15]

From 13 December Fr. Bernardo could no longer stand and was confined to bed. His physical condition deteriorated further; the danger of collapse was obvious from his almost deathly pallor and extreme weakness. On the 18th the superior, warned by the doctor that the end was near, and the confreres urged the Father to prepare to receive the last rites with the sacraments. So they called Fr. Mantuano, his confessor, and Fr. Bernardo, still in the grip of the trial, made his confession “with great and most tender acts of sorrow and compunction”.[16] In his extreme humility, still considering himself unworthy, even incapable, of meeting Jesus in the Eucharist, he asked for time to prepare himself better for holy Viaticum. He knew in spirit that his last hour had not yet come; at the same time he was certain the trial would end with the triumph of grace over temptation, of God over Satan; so he asked them to wait for that hour and explained:

“How can I receive Jesus in the Sacrament with this infernal demon in my bowels?” And to Fr. Mantuano: “You know whether I have ever had difficulty going to confession, having confessed so many times to you and others… I cannot knowingly trample the Blood of Jesus Christ underfoot…”

He renewed his profession of faith, however, and begged them to pray for him that God might prepare him by driving the infernal enemy away from him.[17] But the superior, thinking him on the eve of death, imposed on him a formal precept of obedience to receive the sacraments. And Fr. Bernardo, as if shaken by recourse to such a precept, pleaded in explanation:

“Father Corrector, as a son of obedience I am in your hands. May God dispose it and I am ready. It is not that I do not want to obey; it is that for now I am powerless. You fear I shall die tonight.”

Then, turning to everyone:

“Go and rest, and be at peace; do not doubt, I shall not die tonight, but in this Advent. Tomorrow I shall receive the Sacraments.”[18] “It is not yet time, and I shall not leave you disconsolate. Tomorrow,” he went on “in a meaningful tone”, “will be my feast, because Saint Michael the Archangel will come and overthrow the infernal dragon; then you will see whether I behaved rightly or not.”[19] “My death,” he added, “will be preceded by an earthquake and followed by a storm at sea and on land with lightning, thunder and hail. My death will be known everywhere, and then you will see whether I behaved rightly or not. Go and rest. It is not yet time. Let me recollect myself a little.”[20]

The superior did not insist.[21] No one objected, and they withdrew, except for a priest and a brother who stayed to watch over him.

While the religious were in choir, as Fr. De Gennaro would relate, Fr. Mantuano and this witness were still in Fr. Bernardo’s room trying to persuade him to receive extreme unction, but he kept telling them:

“It is not yet time; leave it to God; this is a mystery and you understand nothing of it; so let God dispose and let me think a little longer.”

And he recollected himself and prayed continually. He was heard calling on the Virgin, more with his breath than his voice, calling her “Mamma mia”.[22]

Meanwhile, from the evening of the 19th, “he was seen to be very calm and free of inner faintings of spirit”;[23] he constantly renewed acts of humility, faith, hope, love and sorrow, and groaned with ever greater intensity:

“Lord, have pity and mercy on this soul of mine. Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.”[24]

It was then, shortly after the midnight change of watch, that Fr. Pranzataro saw him completely calm and, remembering what he had said the evening before, at about 3.30 a.m. asked him whether it was now the “day of salvation”, the hour to receive holy Viaticum. Fr. Bernardo’s message

Bernardo Clausi was neither a writer nor a preacher, though he fully carried out the duties of the sacred ministry. In him outstanding gospel witness shone in concrete daily conduct, and that is mainly where his message lies. He preached, he cried out with his life, as has been said; he wrote in the letters of duty the faithful fulfilment of the Word of God that saves us.

The commandments and precepts, the virtues and the spirit of the beatitudes (the latter as practical criteria and a way of life that makes keeping the former easier), piety and living participation in the liturgy and the sacraments: these were the field of his eloquent message of consistency and fidelity, as well as fervour and perfection.

Fr. Bernardo showed outstanding human and Christian consistency towards God and fervent fidelity to his will, in the wholeness proper to the greatest commandment: with all one’s heart, all one’s soul and all one’s strength. He responded to Christ with sincere and unconditional supernatural adherence and obedience to his gospel. He lived in communion with all members of the Church, beginning with her sacred Pastors, accepting their teaching and discipline. And he professed daily the rule of life embraced by vows in the religious Family of the Minims, following it by vocation, in the spirit of the Founder from Paola, as a specific and sure way of holiness.

For all this Clausi is a thoroughly reliable witness of Christian, religious and priestly life, having experienced first-hand what he also taught as a minister of God and pointed out as a guide and counsellor in the ways of the spirit. His message is therefore sure and convincing, and it reaches beyond his contemporaries into every present day, because of its gospel roots and the authenticity of its transmission.

The specific contents of this message have already appeared in the course of the biography; freed from the contingencies of persons, times and places, they are realities in themselves and values of the highest order. We list the most frequent, handed down by first-hand witnesses and reported in the Venerable’s Processes or found in his writings: the One and Triune God; Jesus and his Eucharistic sacrament; God’s will and his infinite mercy; the Church and the Pope; Our Lady and filial trust in her motherly love and protection; faith, paradise, the supernatural life. These are the most important contents of Fr. Bernardo’s message.

But there is also a series of personal spiritual and ascetical experiences, trials and, in general, inner and outer conduct, in which the message consists of Clausi’s response to the initiative of Grace, to God’s action on him, whether by his will, his permission or his good pleasure. This is the other pole of the example that gives strength and content to Fr. Bernardo’s message. Through it he is not only a witness but a living sign, a point of reference for edification and conduct: a sign of how Grace acts and how the man of God responds.

The message of this witness, favoured by supernatural attraction, and of this living sign, tested by the alternation of light and darkness and the sharpening of tribulation, is indeed manifold and valid; to listen to it is to reflect on his moral and spiritual example in ordinary and extraordinary circumstances, on the way of asceticism and purifying trial, in the successive ascents of the spirit, including the sharpest trial.

“This is the way, this is the trial in which God wants me,” Fr. Bernardo would say, adding: “Who has ever known the ways of God? Who has ever been his counsellor?” and “This is a mystery… Leave it to God.”

The way by which God led him in the crucial period of his greatest trial is among the hardest, tracing the path described by the Mystical Doctor. For a fidelity tested to the utmost, and so more meritorious, the desert of spiritual dryness opened before him. He had to cross it by the light of pure faith, in the deep night, where he experienced loneliness and abandonment. He felt rejected and cast off, yet he did not give way to terror and despair.

Though terribly tried and afflicted by desolation, he held God’s hand constantly, even in the dark, calling on him with unutterable groans, longing for him alone with all the strength of his spirit, sure of seeing the light again in him who hears the cry of the poor. At times God himself inspired this certainty in him, making him a prophet.

After such a trial, Clausi’s example and words carry more weight and his message more credibility. That is why in this appendix we are glad to offer at least an echo of it, gathered from testimony and writings that have come down to us.

Strictly speaking, one cannot talk of a written message of Fr. Bernardo; but we have the elements to compose one, drawn as described.

Meanwhile calm down, be at peace, content and cheerful, for the devil, our enemy, sometimes, and in almost all God’s holy works, tries to disturb us so that we give up good works, because they displease him.

We must bow our heads to God’s just judgements.

I shall not fail to pray to God for you, that he may always give you the grace of victory over the enemy’s malice and cunning.

Fear nothing, for your family will always be under the strong and most powerful intercession and protection of the Most Blessed Virgin of Graces and Mercies.

Meanwhile I shall not fail, and never have failed, to do my duty before the Most High for all of you, unworthy, indeed most unworthy, as I am; so I commend myself also to your holy prayers.

Lord, who are you, and who am I?

Give me my God, and I am well, and I am (as strong as) a Samson.

Credo et firmiter credo.

God is better pleased when alms are given from the best we have.

On the use of talents and gifts:

If a gentleman gives a poor man a purse of money to distribute as alms, whose is the merit, the poor man’s who distributes it or the gentleman’s who gave the money?

It is a work of charity; we must go.

Three things make up my purgatory on earth: writing, riding in a carriage and sitting down.

By God’s grace I have never celebrated with a single venial sin.

Blessed are you, who can love God, draw near to him and receive into your heart a God so good, so lovable!

I cannot understand how people can sin knowingly. God keep me from sin.

The virtue of purity raises people to the throne of God.

Obedience is loved by God.

A day of fasting never killed anyone.

To those who love God nothing is impossible.

Whoever truly has the love of God cannot be unhappy.

I deserve no consideration; I am unworthy of any attention or love; I fully deserve all the pains I suffer and still greater ones. I am a useless servant, a poor peasant by birth. I was a poor soldier; they think I am something, while I am a wretched sinner, a poor little man, the lowest creature on earth. God alone is holy, not I, a poor, miserable sinner.

When applauded or praised:

A most beautiful age will come for the Church, in which many saints will flourish with a special devotion to the Immaculate, such that the Church has never before had so many so devoted to the Immaculate.

I am not worthy to see the world adore this mystery with a defined faith.

Stand firm; be constant in prayer; do not lose heart. Although very sad and dangerous times will come, they will be short: hell will suffer a great defeat, and the divine mercies will come, pouring down from an open sky.

A soul that cost him all the blood of his divine Son is too dear to God.

If only we knew as much as a single hair! But who knows God’s secrets?

Fr. Bernardo, Fr. Bernardo!… Pray to the Lord for me instead, that he may make me good.

Errands are a real cross for me, because one works hard and gets nowhere. I regret the time wasted.

It seems almost ingratitude to leave so many good people who come from morning till evening and almost into the night, and I assure you I truly see the hand of God in it. If you were here, you would be consoled to see the faith and fervour of these good people.

I would not want to leave the work begun half done.

Better to earn little in peace than much with many dangers.

Whoever sows thorns should not go barefoot.

The proverb says that although the fox is the cleverest, fox skins are always for sale; and even the old wolf gets caught in the trap.

The caged bird sings not for love but for rage.

I am well, very well, splendid, in spite of that ugly old devil, despite the hard-working life I have led and still lead.

Let the devil do whatever he likes, for with God’s help he cannot do me any harm… Let him rage, for I do not fear him at all.

I beg you always to be of good heart and cheerful in God, and that in spite of “Don Peppino” (that is, the devil).

In holy works the devil does everything to disturb peace.

Be of good heart and pay no attention to “Don Peppino”; it is a sure sign that you are a soul dear to the Lord, which is why “Don Peppino” is furious.

I lack nothing; indeed I fear the Lord may be paying me in this world. Enough: I want to hope in his divine and infinite mercy.

Pray God, if he pleases, to give me health, and first the salvation of my soul.

So much strain and toil has made me very weak. It is enough that God save my soul through his infinite mercy… May his most holy Will always be done.

I leave the smoke and incense to whoever wants them, content with the roast alone… I have never been obsessed with having my name appear. It is enough for me to have done it for the love of God.

I want always to hope as long as I have breath, so as to do some good work with God’s grace, but meanwhile I make it a sacrifice of good will.

My God, I can give you nothing but what you give me; of myself I have nothing and can offer you only my miseries.

The divine mercies we all long for so much I expect at any moment, and I am surer of them than of my own existence; they will be so great and abundant that we cannot explain or understand them, for they seem not only impossible but unbelievable. When the most fortunate moment comes, then you will say: “Poor Bernardo Clausi was right, though he did not know how to explain himself.”

Rule of life

Always make acts of love of God, of faith, hope, charity, trust, humility and thanksgiving to the Most Holy Trinity, uniting yourself with the whole heavenly Court and the Church militant.

Ask for, seek and desire always holy divine love.

Make aspirations and ejaculatory prayers, and distrust yourself.

Ask always for holy perseverance in loving God.

Often offer the Eternal Father the most precious Blood of his divine Son.

Omnia vincit amor. Qui amat non laborat.

Nil difficile amantibus.

Notes

[saying:] Paradise, Paradise is the only thing to seek, for it is the only true good. Paradise! O Paradise, how beautiful you are; when shall I possess you?

PRAYERS

regularly recited and spread by the Venerable Servant of God Fr. Bernardo M. Clausi

Prayer to the Most Holy Trinity (composed by him)

Eternal Father, here is this wretched, powerless creature who can do nothing: I acknowledge my utter powerlessness and your infinite power; to it I turn in this need of mine, and in it I hope and trust: you take care of it.

Glory be, etc.

Eternal Son, here is this wretched, ignorant creature who knows nothing: I acknowledge my utter ignorance and your infinite wisdom; to it I turn in this need of mine, and in it I trust and abandon myself.

Glory be, etc.

Eternal Holy Spirit, here is this wretched, ungrateful creature who deserves nothing: I acknowledge my utter ingratitude and your infinite goodness; I cling to it; you take care of it; in you I abandon myself, in you I trust.

Glory be, etc.

Prayer of Saint Bernard to the Virgin

Remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, that never was it known that anyone who fled to your protection, implored your help or sought your intercession was left unaided. Inspired by this confidence, I fly to you, O Virgin of virgins, my Mother; to you do I come, before you I stand, sinful and sorrowful. O Mother of the Word Incarnate, despise not my petitions, but in your mercy hear and answer me.

Refugium peccatorum, ora pro nobis. Ave Maria. Consolatrix afflictorum, ora pro nobis. Ave Maria. Auxilium Christianorum, ora pro nobis. Ave Maria.

Trisagion

Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus Deus exercituum. Plena est terra gloria tua. Gloria Patri; Gloria Filio; Gloria Spiritui Sancto.

POEMS OF FR. BERNARDO M. CLAUSI

given to a pupil of the Conservatory degli Orefici in Naples * [literal prose translation of the Italian verse]

I. Repentance

My soul, you are faithless if you do not love your Jesus;

you know well how much you owe him, more than words can tell.

Sin had already killed you; you live by his mercy; and the pardon he promised you he now gives you, lover and king.

Leave the world: it is all deceit when it tries to win your love; shadow, dream, pain and trouble are all it pretends to give.

Yes, my God, I already repent of having offended your goodness;

with shame and contrition I ask only pardon and pity.

If you, Love, will forget my all too faithless deeds,

I promise you, loving God, to live always faithful to you.

Let the world hear me and not expect me to turn back and love it any more; let it know that I have turned my affections to my Jesus.

Yes, yes, truly, truly.

* Cf. APGM, Ven. Clausi, fasc. 6: Varie (with Acta originalia perquisitionis scriptorum, quae Servo Dei P. Bernardo Mariae Clausi tribuuntur, pp. 16, 25-26).

Seek, seek, Carolina, another, more faithful lover;

leave the world which cruelly flattered you and then left you.

You are not alone in this great sorrow; you follow a thousand others; after robbing them of peace, the traitor abandoned them.

You keep a fine heart in your breast, so that you might do Heaven honour;

you are mad if you let yourself be carried away by passion.

Your heart is entangled in the loves you crave; you are a lover, but you do not love the One who alone can satisfy you.

Come, decide, O lovely soul, listen to the One who loves you;

your sorrows are over if you give yourself to devotion!

Leave everything, and in the bosom of God, who is a faithful and sincere lover, go… rest… and, if you persevere, you will find happiness.

III. Warning

If love plays around you, do not think yourself happy: one day you will see your mistake for what it is.

The lover you believe in only wants to laugh at you; O foolish girl, you do not see the betrayal of your trust!

He swears and forswears, and meanwhile his promises are fleeting; mad is anyone who trusts the deceitful world so much!

How many fairer than you has the traitor led astray;

for the wolf among the lambs was always a traitor!

He too boasts of being faithful, but it is dream, passion and frenzy;

there is nothing else to enchant you; it binds your freedom!

So understand at last, my lover, and, simple soul, surrender: only God, constant love, is joy and faithfulness! Farewell.

HYMNS

formerly sung in the Venerable’s parish at SAN SISTO DEI VALDESI* [literal prose translation of the Italian verse]

1) Hymn in honour of the Most Holy Trinity

Praised for ever be the Most Holy Trinity, who always loved Mary with the fullness of divine goodness.

The Most Holy Trinity made her Mother of the Messiah, set her above all others and gave her every dignity.

The Most Holy Trinity exalted her with song and gave her lordship over all powers.

The Trinity then made her a worthy and loving Advocate, and willed that she should always be for us a Mother of mercy.

This rhymed composition is also found, with some variations, in a letter of Clausi to Sr. M. Cherubina della Passione (cf. Archive of the Perpetual Adorers in Rome).

The Venerable would sometimes hum this and similar hymns in his tuneful voice.

So let us turn to Mary, that she may pray to the Trinity to help us on this road to eternal happiness.

We turn to you, Mary, to enjoy the Trinity; let this be the holiness of us all.

Turn your eyes of charity, loving Mother, on the Church, that she may be kept far from all adversity.

Grant too that charity may always be alive among us and on earth be always a strong spur to devotion.

Praised for ever be Mary’s purity, and Jesus be praised for all eternity.

2) Lullaby for the Child Jesus*

Sleep, sleep, beloved and dear, close your eyes, fair soul; ah, comfort your handmaid, I beg you for pity’s sake.

Hush-a-bye, lullaby, hush-a-bye, lullaby.

I know he sleeps while his heart keeps watch, for he is man and true God; sleep then, sleep, my lovely one, sleep in perfect freedom.

Hush-a-bye, etc.

You will always be attended by sovereign cherubim, yet persecuted by afflicted humanity.

Hush-a-bye, etc.

All you Angels of the highest Heaven, gather round, for he is asleep; form a choir with your melody and attend His Majesty. Hush-a-bye, etc.

Sleep, sleep, beloved and dear, now that you are a child, for in the hands of your enemies there will be no more sleep. Hush-a-bye, etc.

Blow, zephyrs, gentle breezes, for the divine Father already rejoices; bring comfort to the great Son of the supreme Godhead. Hush-a-bye, etc.

* In the original in G. Caracciolo’s manuscript “Raccolta” (in the private family archive of Emilio Gonzales), the refrain reads “Ninna nonna” instead of “Ninna nanna”, following local usage.

Blows, thorns, harsh cords, crosses, spittle and horrid blindfolds you will suffer, so that Heaven will not shine at the sight of such cruelty.

Hush-a-bye, etc.

When you suffer such pains, my dear Son, in that dreadful peril there will be no more sleep. Hush-a-bye, etc.

You will see even Kings prostrate at your feet, but a monarch will wage cruel war on you out of envy.

Hush-a-bye, etc.

Keep watch, O Seraphim, now that my love is sleeping, for he is Son of the great God who reigns in Heaven. Hush-a-bye, etc.

While you lie in the cradle, my sweetest treasure, the Angels will praise in chorus the Majesty in the little child.

Hush-a-bye, etc.

The time will come when you will act as God who rules all things, but the ungrateful, faithless flock will scorn to adore you.

Hush-a-bye, etc.

You will grow day by day, lovely, lovable and innocent, but your faithless people will look on you as a criminal.

Hush-a-bye, etc.

After so much bitter suffering you will at last die on the wood, to give a new sign to afflicted humanity.

Hush-a-bye, etc.

Notes

* Cf. APGM, Ven. Clausi, fasc. 6: Varie.

SACRED HYMNS OF SILVIO PELLICO

brought to San Sisto dei Valdesi by the Venerable Fr. Bernardo M. Clausi * [literal prose translation of the Italian verse]

1) To the Sacred Heart of Mary

Heart of Mary, whom the Angels admire as the heart in which, after the Lord, the greatest goodness shines.

You are the heart of a tender Mother to the innocent, and also to the sinner who groans and hopes in your mercy.

Earth and Heaven honour you; the King your Son honours you; you are the spotless lily the serpent did not spoil.

From your virgin blood was formed the beautiful heart of the adored Lamb who ransomed the world.

* Taken from G. Caracciolo’s manuscript “Raccolta” cited above, where they are copied over Silvio Pellico’s signature, these are unpublished pieces Clausi is said to have received directly from the author at one of their meetings in Turin, at the Barolo castle of the Marquises Falletti, or at Chieri at the home of his sister Giuseppina Pellico.

Hail then the glorious Heart of the Great Queen, before whom man and seraph bow as subjects.

Take my heart, O Virgin, you can transform it; give it your affections, give it your divine Love.

The Heart of Christ rejoices over your most pure Heart; never were two hearts more alike in love.

How can we fail to offer you pleasing homage, we children weakened by faults and fear?

Come to me, my children (so Mary answers). I cannot turn away anyone who pours out so many prayers.

Gather close around me, stay always by my side; I shall cover you with my mantle and be your defence.

2) The soul and the guardian angel

Soul: Little Angel of my God, I am not worthy of you; little Angel of my God, what are you doing near me?

Angel: I am the friend of your heart, an Angel of the Lord; when you wake and when you sleep, always, always I am with you.

Soul: Little Angel of my God, I am not worthy of you; little Angel of my God, do you not know that I am weak?

Angel: I know your clay is frail, I know your sight is weak; I pity and help you; hope and love, and you will be forgiven.

Soul: Little Angel of my God, I am not worthy of you; little Angel of my God, I would like to fly with you.

Angel: If you want the wings of fervour, let the Virgin be your love; a mind faithful to her can rise to Heaven.

Soul: Little Angel of my God, I am not worthy of you; little Angel of my God, I would like to please Mary.

Angel: To please my Queen, leave the world and set out in her Son’s footsteps on the way of the Cross.

Soul: Little Angel of my God, I am not worthy of you; little Angel of my God, Ah, Jesus, tell me where he is?…

Angel: He is in Heaven and on the Altar; you can find him in yourself; whoever trusts in him breathes him; whoever loves him well has him within.

Soul: Little Angel of my God, I am not worthy of you; little Angel of my God, do you approve of fear?…

Angel: Fear, yes, but as a daughter who dares raise her eyes to her Father; let it be a yearning full of love, a sigh of virtue.

Soul: Little Angel of my God, I am not worthy of you; little Angel of my God, joy floods my heart.

Angel: Laugh, yes, but let your smile be the joy of Paradise, the gladness of a pure soul that stays at Christ’s feet.

Soul: Little Angel of my God, I am not worthy of you; little Angel of my God, give me your heart; I give you mine.

Angel: I take yours; you have mine; may they never be parted. Ah, let us form one heart for him who created us.
